title: Napa Valley
description: A small valley north of San Francisco that put American wine on the world map, built on Cabernet Sauvignon.
L: Napa Valley lies about 80 km north of San Francisco, about 50 km long and a few kilometres wide, between the Mayacamas Mountains to the west and the Vaca Range to the east. It has about 18,000 hectares of vines, only about 4% of California's, but a large share of its value. Soils are extremely varied: over 30 types.
50 km long, about 4% of California's vines

Napa has a Mediterranean climate: dry, warm summers and mild, wet winters. Cool air and fog come in from San Pablo Bay in the south each night and morning, so the southern end, Carneros, is coolest, and the northern end, Calistoga, hottest. The daily fog keeps acidity in grapes that ripen fully under strong sun.
Why is Carneros cooler than Calistoga?
It's closer to San Pablo Bay and its fog
Bay fog and cool air reach the south first.

Vines were planted in Napa in the 1830s; by the 1880s, there were over 140 wineries. Phylloxera and Prohibition, from 1920 to 1933, nearly ended the industry. In 1966, Robert Mondavi founded the first major new winery since Prohibition, and modern Napa grew from there. In 1968, Napa created the Agricultural Preserve, protecting land from development.
Napa Valley makes most of California's wine by volume.
Not true. It has only about 4% of California's vineyards, though its wines are among the most valuable.
Napa is a small valley between two mountain ranges
Bay fog cools the south; the north is hotter

Cabernet Sauvignon is Napa's star, about 40% of vineyards and most of its value. Napa Cabernet is ripe and powerful, with blackcurrant, black cherry, cassis, chocolate and mint, ripe tannins and often 14.5% alcohol or more, aged in new French oak. Bordeaux-style blends are called Meritage, a trademarked term.

Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot and Malbec join Cabernet in blends. Chardonnay is the main white, especially in cooler Carneros. Sauvignon Blanc, sometimes called Fumé Blanc, a name Mondavi coined, and Zinfandel also grow. Pinot Noir thrives in Carneros.
Napa Cabernet grapes are among the most expensive in the world, often over 10,000 dollars per tonne for top vineyards.
About 40% of vineyards and most of the value.
Bordeaux grapes join it in blends called Meritage
Chardonnay and Pinot Noir thrive in cool Carneros

On 24 May 1976, British wine merchant Steven Spurrier organised a blind tasting in Paris. Nine French judges compared top Californian wines with top Bordeaux reds and Burgundy whites. Spurrier expected the French wines to win. A journalist from Time magazine, George Taber, was there.

In the whites, Chateau Montelena's 1973 Chardonnay, from Napa, came first, ahead of Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet. In the reds, Stag's Leap Wine Cellars' 1973 Cabernet Sauvignon came first, ahead of Mouton Rothschild and Haut-Brion. Time reported it as the Judgment of Paris.
Which Napa Cabernet won the red section in 1976?
Chateau Montelena won the whites with Chardonnay.

The result shocked France and gave California, and the New World, credibility. Investment poured into Napa. A rematch in 2006, with the same wines aged 30 years, again placed Californian reds on top. The story became the film Bottle Shock in 2008. Bottles from the tasting are in the Smithsonian museum.
What were the effects of the Judgment of Paris?
It banned French wine in the US
Steven Spurrier's 1976 blind tasting compared California and France
Chateau Montelena and Stag's Leap won
It gave the New World credibility
Compare valley floor and mountain sites

An AVA, American Viticultural Area, is a defined grape-growing area; a label naming one must use at least 85% of grapes from it. Napa Valley AVA was created in 1981, California's first. Within it are 16 smaller AVAs, each with distinct soils and climate. Napa County law also requires at least 75% Napa Valley grapes for wines naming a Napa sub-AVA.

Valley floor AVAs include Oakville and Rutherford, with alluvial soils, famous for rich Cabernet; Rutherford is known for its dusty, earthy Rutherford dust; and Stags Leap District, with softer, elegant tannins. Mountain AVAs, like Howell Mountain, Mount Veeder, Spring Mountain and Diamond Mountain, sit above the fog, with thin, volcanic soils, giving more structured, tannic wines.
Match each AVA to its feature.
Each AVA has its own character.

Napa's AVAs show that even a small valley has big differences in soil and climate. Mountain sites, above the fog line, get more sun but cooler temperatures, and lower yields. Valley floor sites are warmer and more fertile. Many top wines blend from several AVAs; others come from single vineyards, like To Kalon in Oakville.
What must a wine contain to name an AVA on its label?
At least 85% grapes from that AVA
Napa Valley AVA, created in 1981, contains 16 sub-AVAs
Valley floor AVAs give rich wines; mountain AVAs structured ones
A label naming an AVA needs at least 85% of its grapes
Reading Napa and eating with it

Labels show the winery, the grape, at least 75% of it by US law, the AVA, at least 85%, and the vintage, at least 95% from that year. Estate Bottled means the winery grew and made the wine within the AVA. Reserve has no legal meaning. Cult wines, like Screaming Eagle and Harlan Estate, are made in tiny quantities and sell for very high prices.

Napa Cabernet suits steak, especially grilled ribeye, lamb, beef short ribs and hard cheeses. Its ripe fruit and tannin need fat and protein. Napa Chardonnay suits lobster, crab and roast chicken. Serve Cabernet at 16 to 18 degrees, decanted when young. Top Napa Cabernet ages 15 to 30 years.
What does Reserve mean on a Napa label?
In the US, Reserve isn't regulated.
Napa's wineries welcome millions of visitors a year. Many tastings are by appointment, so book ahead.
Estate Bottled means the winery grew and made the wine within the AVA.
Labels follow 75% grape, 85% AVA, 95% vintage rules
Napa Cabernet suits steak and lamb
